I acknowledge the answer. I am convinced by the authors' answer about the training of the classifier. 

I will keep my rating as is. I find the method interesting and experimental results are convincing. However, the proposed solution requires feature engineering and thus might no be very generic (extension to other type of image datasets or other modalities is not guaranteed to work). That is why I do not raise my score to Accept.

**[Q1] Overall this work is very interesting, but I would really like to see more experiments beyond pixel-space consistency models (e.g., latent consistency training on ImageNet 256), where LPIPS is unavailable and AYT could potentially demonstrate its real strength.**

We conducted experiments to evaluate our method in the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) setting. We trained both Easy Consistency Training (ECT) and our method on ImageNet 512×512 for 50k iterations with a batch size of 128, initializing from the same pretrained EDM2 checkpoint. We used SD-VAE as the latent autoencoder. The overall experimental configuration follows the setup used for ImageNet 64×64, with two key differences: multi-stage training was not applied, and the timestep sampling distribution was modified to match the EDM2 configuration for ImageNet 512×512. To train the manifold feature model, we employed the following data augmentations: scale, anisotropy, rotation, translation, blur, mixup, and noise.

As shown in Table below, our method shows improvement compared to original ECT baseline on quality metrics such as FID and IS while showing comparable results on diversity metrics such as Recall and Coverage, proving our method is also viable on latent domain. We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.1 for a detailed explanation.

|Metric | FID | IS | Precision | Recall | Density | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 27.479 | 27.55 | 0.77 | 0.58 | 0.63  | 0.89 |
| AYT | 27.029 | 27.85 | 0.77 | 0.58 | 0.63  | 0.88 |

**[Q2] In Fig. 3, how are the M parallel and M orth components computed? If you can decompose the two directions without AYT, why not just suppress the parallel component directly?**

In Fig. 3, we use a synthetic dataset with known manifold structure such that we can explicitly decompose the tangent into manifold parallel and orthogonal components by computing the tangent space of the manifold at a given space. That said, for the real world dataset such as CIFAR10 or ImageNet, we do not know the underlying manifold for explicit decomposition as suggested by the reviewer.

Thank you for your reply! We provide further discussion to address your concerns (highlighted in bold) point by point.

> **I do not find the experiments in Appendix. B.4 convincing evidence that the level sets of the learned feature map “recover the data manifold.” What you actually show there is much more limited: starting from perturbations or transformations of a single data point, you optimize over the transformation parameter and recover that same point. Recovering a single training data point does not demonstrate that the gradient is orthogonal to the manifold, so it does not support the proposed method.**

We gently remind the Reviewer that in Figure 8 (Appendix B.4) of our revised manuscript, we have already shown that manifold inversion recovers the perturbed data manifold for multiple samples. Furthermore, in Figure 4 (Section 4) of our main paper, we demonstrate that manifold feature gradients are orthogonal to the data manifold.

> **To me, the claimed connection between the feature-based distance and manifold recovery is mostly intuitive rather than supported by the experiments. There is also no theorem or formal proposition that theoretically backs this intuition**

We refer the Reviewer to Appendix C of our revised manuscript, where now provide a formal proof of manifold-orthogonality of manifold feature gradients.

> **Empirically, the feature-based loss brings limited gains over the ECT baseline, mostly in terms of the one-step FID score case. However, the two-step FID does not outperform the baseline.**

We first remark that the degradation in two-step FIDs is really marginal compared to the large gains in one-step FIDs. For instance, on CIFAR10, we improve one-step FID from 3.60 to 2.61 (FID gain of ~1.0) while suffering from a slight loss in two-step FID from 2.11 to 2.13 (FID loss of 0.02). On ImageNet 64x64, we improve one-step FID from 5.51 to 4.42 (FID gain of ~1.1) with a slight loss in two-step FID from 3.18 to 3.27 (FID loss of 0.09).

Moreover, on some metrics, our method outperforms the baseline in terms of both one and two-step FIDs. In Table 3, on CIFAR10, one/two-step Inception Scores improve from 9.80/10.09 to 9.98/10.16 and on ImageNet 64x64, one/two-step Inception Scores improve from 17.17/21.35 to 19.00/22.22.

Finally, we would like to remind the Reviewer and emphasize our contributions. First, AYT yields substantial performance gains with minimal changes: it improves 1-step FID by about 1.0 on CIFAR-10 and 1.1 on ImageNet-64 simply by computing the CM loss on manifold features. In contrast, several accepted consistency model papers achieve smaller gains (~0.8 and ~0.4 for sCT [4], ~0.9 and ~0.5 for ECT-GC [5] respectively) despite requiring many architectural and training modifications. Second, in addition to the generative performance improvement, AYT accelerates convergence (x10 in terms of number of CM training iterations, and x3.9 in terms of wall-clock time) and enables stable training with extremely small batch sizes (our CM trained with batch size 16 beats the ECT baseline trained with batch size 128). We believe this is a non-trivial contribution given that CM training is notoriously unstable [1,2,3,4].

**Given these contributions, we respectfully argue that it is unjustified to dismiss our work with repeated claims of “limited FID gains” without recognizing the broader improvements our method introduces.**

[1] Consistency Models, ICML 2023.

[2] Stabilizing the Training of Consistency Models with Score Guidance, ICML 2024 Workshop

[3] Improved Techniques for Training Consistency Models, ICLR, 2024

[4] Simplifying, Stabilizing and Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models, ICLR, 2025

[5] Improving Consistency Models with Generator-Augmented Flows, ICML, 2025

> **The visual quality of the generation in Figure 10 can easily find cases where baseline generation is better. So it might be that the feature-based loss is beneficial for a better FID score (also feature-based), but not much for actual better generation.**

We first remark that **“visual quality of a sample” is a very subjective criterion** which can vary largely individual by individual, and that is **why we use objective quantitative metrics such as FID, IS, etc**. Furthermore, samples shown in Figure 10 are a very small subset of the 50000 samples used to calculate FID, IS, etc., so one cannot claim baseline is better simply because **some baseline samples have “better visual quality” than our samples.** If the Reviewer is not satisfied with the FID score, we kindly remind the Reviewer that we have also reported other metrics such as IS, precision, recall, density, coverage on which our method also shows competitive or better scores (Table 3 in Appendix B).

summary.value: Paper identifies a key problem in training Consistency Models (CMs): "tangent oscillation." The authors find that near convergence, the CM's output update directions often move parallel to the manifold, leading to slow convergence. Authors propose a novel, self-supervised loss function called the Manifold Feature Distance (MFD) (by training an auxiliary feature extractor).  AYT outperform the popular LPIPS loss function, and achieve state-of-the-art FID scores on CIFAR10 and ImageNet $64 \times 64$.

strengths.value:
- The "oscillatory tangent hypothesis"  is a well-supported insight into a key problem (slow/unstable convergence) in SOTA consistency models.
- Theoretical framework of MFD, i.e. Gradients and level sets, is plausible. 
- Small batch-sized stable training of CMs is a meaningful contribution. 
- Failure modes of LPIPS are clearly discussed and addressed in proposed self-supervised alternative.

weaknesses.value:
- The new step of pre-training the auxiliary feature extractor $\phi$ is described as "lightweight", but the appendix states it is trained for 400k iterations. The "lightweight" claim is not sufficiently quantified in terms of actual compute/flops or wall-clock time relative to the main CM training 
- The feature extractor is a VGG16 (which is indeed a common choice for getting manifold), a choice seemingly inherited from LPIPS. The paper does not ablate this choice. How sensitive are the results to this specific architecture? Would a simpler, custom CNN work? Which would bolster the "lightweight" claim? Or does the method rely on the specific inductive biases of VGG?
- All experiments were run on low-resolution images, how does the performance change with increasing resolution? 
- Evaluation focuses on just FID. No precision/recall, coverage/density, or aesthetic/CLIP-based metrics. 
- (Eq. 9-14) concludes that the AYT tangent is a linear combination of the feature gradients, and that $\nabla \phi_i$ are manifold-orthogonal by construction. However, the weighting terms, $d\phi_i/dt$, are highly dynamic, as they depend on the time derivative of the CM's own output $f_\theta(x_t, t)$ as it moves through the feature space. What mathematical proof or analysis guarantees that this weighted sum remains robustly manifold-orthogonal? How does authors make sure that the weights, $d\phi_i/dt$, cannot create a specific combination that gives a vector with a dominant manifold-parallel component, thereby re-introducing the very oscillation you aim to solve?

summary.value: This manuscript focuses on analyzing the training dynamics of consistency models, and proposes to mitigate oscillating updates by introducing a manifold-aware feature space objective that improves training stability. In-depth theoretical analysis is presented, showing that CM training's update direction (called "tangents") are not orthogonal to the data manifold, but contains oscillating parallel components, which impairs convergence. A feature space distance is then proposed to align the tangents with the orthogonal direction, which employs a network trained on corrupted image data. This achieves similar performance to using LPIPS loss but without human labeling.

strengths.value:
- The most significant contribution in this paper is showing that LPIPS loss in consistency models can be replaced by a self-supervised network to achieve the comparable performance. This potentially enables applying feature space loss in consistency models outside the image domain, overcoming the scarcity LPIPS-like metrics in other modalities.
- The design of the feature space metric makes is technically sound. Ablations of different types of transformations also reveal that geometric transformation is the most important, potentially indicating that structural awareness is the most important update direction in consistency models. 
- The analysis on training update directions ("tangents") is solid and provides an interesting perspective of understanding consistency training.
- Overall, the quality of this manuscript is high, both in terms of technical details and writing clarity.

weaknesses.value:
- The experiments do not show any significant advantage of the proposed method over existing ones. The comparison with LPIPS does not reveal a very clear gap. In Fig. 5, the FID scores are very close. This is a major limit to the significance the contribution. In addition, both LPIPS and AYT are starting to get worse after 250k iterations, so argument that "CM trained with LPIPS showed degradation in two-step FIDs after 200k iterations." could also apply to AYT similarly.
- The statement that "We discover a potential cause of slow convergence in CM training" is a bit over-claiming. While this manuscript provides an interesting perspective based-on data manifold, the slow convergence in CT is well-understood: CM's target x0 is propagated from the boundary condition at t=0 to intermediate times, causing accumulation of errors, which naturally includes noisy components that impairs training stability.

Thank you for your reply. I do not find the experiments in Appendix. B.4 convincing evidence that the level sets of the learned feature map “recover the data manifold.” What you actually show there is much more limited: starting from perturbations or transformations of a single data point, you optimize over the transformation parameter and recover that same point. There is also no theorem or formal proposition that theoretically backs this intuition, and empirically, the feature-based loss brings limited gains over the ECT baseline, mostly in terms of the one-step FID score case. However, the two-step FID does not outperform the baseline, and the visual quality of the generation in Figure 10 can easily find cases where baseline generation is better. So it might be that the feature-based loss is beneficial for a better FID score (also feature-based), but not much for actual better generation.

**[W1] Experiments on CIFAR10 in Section 4 are less convincing. It is only based on visualizations, which are not easily interpretable. I am uncertain if conclusions can be drawn from these visualizations.**

We assure the Reviewer that CIFAR10 visualizations in Section 4 are not used as hard evidence of the oscillatory tangent hypothesis. In fact, as clarified in lines 239-241 of our paper, the visualizations are only used as motivating observation for the hypothesis.
Also, we fully agree with the Reviewer that CIFAR10 experiments in Section 4 does not provide hard evidence of the oscillatory tangent hypothesis, and that is why we have also performed a rigorous analysis with a synthetic dataset with known manifold structure. Indeed, on the synthetic dataset of two-dimensional discs, we have observed that CMs near convergence exhibit oscillatory tangents which move CM outputs along the data manifold, not towards the manifold.

**[W2] Although the training of the generative model is faster, it relies on pre-training classifiers for the feature map construction. Moreover, it seems that it is required to train one classifier for each feature. This makes the overall pipeline complex, and the compute budget probably higher than in the original model.**

We assure the Reviewer that the training pipeline remains simple, since we use one classifier with $n>1$-dimensional outputs to learn several manifold features in parallel. For example, if we were to learn manifold features for Gaussian noise addition (parametrized by standard deviation of added Gaussian noise $\sigma_1$) and Gaussian blurring (parametrized by standard deviation of blur kernel $\sigma_2$), the classifier output dimension would be $2$, with the first coordinate predicting $\sigma_1$ and the second coordinate predicting $\sigma_2$.

Furthermore, as shown in Table 1 of our revised paper, AYT offers up to 3.9 times acceleration in wall-clock time even when taking classifier training into account. Hence, AYT saves compute budget when compared to the baseline ECT.

**[Q1] To construct the several features, could you rely on a classifier with several heads?**

We indeed rely on a classifier with several heads, as written in our reply to Weakness 2 of this review.

**[W1] The new step of pre-training the auxiliary feature extractor is described as "lightweight", but the appendix states it is trained for 400k iterations. The "lightweight" claim is not sufficiently quantified in terms of actual compute/flops or wall-clock time relative to the main CM training.**

We refer the Reviewer to Table 1 of the revised manuscript, where we show that even when including training of the auxiliary feature extractor, AYT is up to 3.9 times faster than baseline ECT in terms of wall-clock time.

**[W2] The feature extractor is a VGG16 (which is indeed a common choice for getting manifolds), a choice seemingly inherited from LPIPS. The paper does not ablate this choice. How sensitive are the results to this specific architecture? Would a simpler, custom CNN work? Which would bolster the "lightweight" claim? Or does the method rely on the specific inductive biases of VGG?**

We refer the Reviewer to Section 6.1 lines 417 - 426, where we show that simpler custom CNNs as manifold features provide similar or slightly better performance than VGG. We also show that more complex architectures such as ResNet or DenseNet degrade performance, implying simple architectures work best as manifold features.

**[W3] All experiments were run on low-resolution images, how does the performance change with increasing resolution?**

We conducted experiments to evaluate our method in the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) setting. We trained both Easy Consistency Training (ECT) and our method on ImageNet 512×512 for 50k iterations with a batch size of 128, initializing from the same pretrained EDM2 checkpoint. We used SD-VAE as the latent autoencoder. The overall experimental configuration follows the setup used for ImageNet 64×64, with two key differences: multi-stage training was not applied, and the timestep sampling distribution was modified to match the EDM2 configuration for ImageNet 512×512. To train the manifold feature model, we employed the following data augmentations: scale, anisotropy, rotation, translation, blur, mixup, and noise.

As shown in Table below, our method shows improvement compared to original ECT baseline on quality metrics such as FID and IS while showing comparable results on diversity metrics such as Recall and Coverage, proving our method is also viable on latent domain. We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.1 for a detailed explanation.

|Metric | FID | IS | Precision | Recall | Density | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 27.479 | 27.55 | 0.77 | 0.58 | 0.63  | 0.89 |
| AYT | 27.029 | 27.85 | 0.77 | 0.58 | 0.63  | 0.88 |

**[W4] Evaluation focuses on just FID. No precision/recall, coverage/density, or aesthetic/CLIP-based metrics.**

We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.1 of our revised manuscript, where we report additional metrics such as the Inception Score, precision, recall, density, coverage. We find that AYT yields competitive scores on the additional metrics as well. In particular, AYT improves quality metrics such as FID, Inception Score, precision, and density, while preserving diversity metrics such as recall and coverage. This implies AYT does not sacrifice diversity to improve sample quality.

**[W5] (Eq. 9-14) concludes that the AYT tangent is a linear combination of the feature gradients, and that $\nabla \phi_i$ are manifold-orthogonal by construction. However, the weighting terms, $d\phi_i/dt$, are highly dynamic, as they depend on the time derivative of the CM's own output  as it moves through the feature space. What mathematical proof or analysis guarantees that this weighted sum remains robustly manifold-orthogonal? How do authors make sure that the weights, $d\phi_i/dt$, cannot create a specific combination that gives a vector with a dominant manifold-parallel component, thereby re-introducing the very oscillation you aim to solve?**

We assure the Reviewer that any linear combination of feature gradients is still manifold-orthogonal. This follows by linear algebra. Specifically, let us assume that each $\nabla \phi_i$ are manifold-orthogonal (which follows by definition of manifold features). Let $c_i$ be an arbitrary choice of coefficients, and also let $v$ be an arbitrary manifold-parallel vector. Then, $v \cdot \nabla \phi_i = 0$ (here, $\cdot$ denotes inner product) since each feature gradient is manifold-orthogonal. It follows that $v \cdot \sum_i c_i \nabla \phi_i = \sum_i c_i v \cdot \nabla \phi_i = \sum_i c_i \times 0 = 0$ by linearity of inner product. Because $v$ is an arbitrary manifold-parallel vector, this shows that $\sum_i c_i \nabla \phi_i$ is manifold-orthogonal, and because $c_i$ are arbitrary coefficients, this shows that any linear combination of manifold feature gradients is manifold-orthogonal.


**[Q1] Looking forward to the authors' response on the proof of manifold-orthogonality.**

We refer the Reviewer to our answer to Weakness 5, where we provide a proof of manifold-orthogonality.

summary.value: The paper discusses the tangent oscillation in the training of the consistency model and proposes a method to align the tangent to the data manifold.

strengths.value: The training of the consistency model is an interesting question. The authors made an effort to advocate for a representation space-based loss might be beneficial.

weaknesses.value:
1. The oscillatory tangent hypothesis is not very convincing. It is not clear what to be concerned about if we see some components of the tangent are tangent to the manifold. Note that the goal of the diffusion model or consistency model is not just to generate samples on the data manifold, but also to learn the data distribution. So some components of the "tangent" that are tangent to the manifold may just be needed to adjust for the distributional correctness and not necessarily a problem.
2. The notion of manifold feature is the center of the paper. However, it is not clearly validated. For example, does the level set $\phi^{-1}(x) = \alpha$ recovers the data manifold? If that is the case, then it seems to be able to perform gradient descent on the cost $||\phi(x) - \alpha||$ to obtain a data point on the manifold. 
3. I am a bit confused about the experiments setup, as far as I understand, the ECT do use a pertained model and if the paper follows the same setup, then one cannot claim improvement over distillation based models. 
4. The novelty of introducing a representation space-based loss is rather limited. The performance gain is not very significant.

**[W4] The novelty of introducing a representation space-based loss is rather limited.**

In contrast to the Reviewer’s concern, our work contains novel insights compared to previous works on using representations to improve diffusion or flow training, as discussed in Section 2 of our paper. We provide further discussion below. This text is included as Appendix C.3 in our updated manuscript.

*Comparison to representation alignment.* Motivations behind representation alignment type of works such as [1,2] and our work are fundamentally different. The former aims to enhance generative quality of diffusion and flow models by aligning the internal representations of diffusion and flow models to high-quality self-supervised representations. As the authors of REPA wrote in their paper (see Appendix M of [1]), there is no solid theoretical intuition as to why representation alignment helps flow and diffusion training. On the other hand, our work pinpoints a source of slow convergence in CMs (Section 4), namely oscillatory tangents, and derives a theoretically principled loss for mitigating them (Section 5).

*Comparison to previous perceptual losses.* The most relevant works to ours are [3] and [4]. Research on perceptual objectives for Consistency Models (CMs) has been limited since the original CM paper. Following the introduction of the pseudo-Huber loss in [5] as an alternative to LPIPS, subsequent CM studies have largely continued to employ pseudo-Huber loss or closely related variants without significant changes. Although perceptual objectives have been shown to improve generative quality in diffusion models—for example, in the aforementioned works—they have been underexplored in the context of CMs despite their potential benefits.

*Comparison to previous consistency model works.* Our contribution is twofold: we revisit perceptual objectives for CMs and improve upon LPIPS-based formulations, and we also identify the previously unaddressed issue of tangent oscillation during training. Existing CM research has primarily focused on reducing error accumulation—for example, by modifying model architecture [6], minimizing discretization errors via JVP techniques [6,7], leveraging pretrained diffusion models or performing additional stages for stabilized initialization [6,8,9], or introducing curriculum learning strategies [10].

These approaches all aim to reduce accumulated error across timesteps, but they do not account for the oscillatory behavior we observe in manifold-parallel tangent components. By uncovering this distinct source of slow convergence, we provide a complementary perspective and a novel direction for improving CM training stability. A related line of work is [11], but unlike that work, our method focuses more directly on the geometric structure of the data manifold.

[1] Representation Alignment for Generation: Training Diffusion Transformers Is Easier Than You Think, ICLR, 2025.

[2] REPA-E: Unlocking VAE for End-to-End Tuning with Latent Diffusion Transformers, arXiv, 2025.

[3] Diffusion Model with Perceptual Loss, arXiv, 2024.

[4] Boosting Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Objectives, ICLR, 2025.

[5] Improved Techniques for Training Consistency Models, ICLR, 2024.

[6] Simplifying, Stabilizing and Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models, ICLR, 2025.

[7]  Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling, arXiv, 2025.

[8] Consistency Models Made Easy, ICLR, 2025.

[9] CMT: Mid-Training for Efficient Learning of Consistency, Mean Flow, and Flow Map Models, arXIv, 2025.

[10] AlphaFlow: Understanding and Improving MeanFlow Models, arXiv, 2025.

[11] Improving Consistency Models with Generator-Augmented Flows, ICML, 2025.

**[W5] The performance gain is not significant.**

We also assure the Reviewer that the performance gain from AYT is non-trivial. For instance, sCT [1] provides 1-step FID gains of ~0.8 on CIFAR10 and ~0.4 on ImageNet 64x64 compared to ECT with major changes such as conversion from discrete to continuous setup, architectural changes (adaptive double normalization, positional embedding), adaptive loss weighting, tangent warmup, etc. On the other hand, AYT provides 1-step FID gains of ~1.0 on CIFAR10 and ~1.1 on ImageNet 64x64 compared to ECT simply by computing CM loss with manifold features.

[1] Simplifying, Stabilizing and Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models, ICLR, 2025.

**[Q1] Can you clarify your training procedure?**

We refer the Reviewer to our answer to Weakness 3, where we clarify that ECT and AYT beats distillation in terms of both training efficiency and generative performance.

**[Q2] Can you validate the manifold feature used in practice?**

We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.4 of our revised paper, where we show that manifold feature level sets indeed approximate perturbed data manifolds by the method suggested by the Reviewer.

**[W2] The statement that "We discover a potential cause of slow convergence in CM training" is a bit over-claiming. While this manuscript provides an interesting perspective based-on data manifold, the slow convergence in CT is well-understood: CM's target x0 is propagated from the boundary condition at t=0 to intermediate times, causing accumulation of errors, which naturally includes noisy components that impairs training stability.**

We agree with the Reviewer, and have revised the sentence (line 80) to “We perform a rigorous analysis of the slow convergence in CM training”. In fact, we believe error propagation and oscillatory tangents are not orthogonal views on the slow convergence of CMs. Propagated error mentioned by the Reviewer may manifest as oscillation of tangents, so our method can be interpreted as an effort to reduce propagated error and provide better regression targets for CM outputs at large time $t$.

Furthermore, error accumulation is also observed in Consistency Distillation (CD), yet it is well-documented that Consistency Training (CT) converges more slowly and often underperforms CD. This discrepancy indicates that factors beyond simple error propagation contribute to CT's instability. Our perspective based on tangent oscillation provides a complementary explanation of this discrepancy.

**[W1] The oscillatory tangent hypothesis is not very convincing. It is not clear what to be concerned about if we see some components of the tangent are parallel to the manifold. Note that the goal of the diffusion model or consistency model is not just to generate samples on the data manifold, but also to learn the data distribution. So some components of the "tangent" that are parallel to the manifold may just be needed to adjust for the distributional correctness and not necessarily a problem.**

We agree with the Reviewer that manifold-parallel components are also crucial for generating diverse samples, and that is why, to train the manifold feature model, we employed various data augmentations that degrade image quality such as scale, anisotropy, rotation, translation, blur, mixup, and noise. Accordingly, **components of the “tangent” that are amplified by AYT tends to be image degradations, and distinct from directions necessary for diverse generation on the data manifold**. Therefore, our method encouraged to focus on restoring these corrupted details. This design naturally places greater emphasis on correcting off-manifold deviations while still preserving essential on-manifold information.

Moreover, a prior work (Theorem 2 in [1]) has shown that, when the loss exhibits a well-defined Hessian, Consistency Training (CT) is theoretically guaranteed to fit the underlying data distribution. This implies that our additional regularization does not prevent the model from learning the correct distribution; rather, it stabilizes the training dynamics by mitigating undesirable oscillations near convergence. In other words, our method should be understood as improving optimization stability without compromising distributional fidelity.

Finally, in Table 3 in Appendix A of our revised manuscript, we observe AYT yields competitive values for diversity metrics recall and coverage when compared to ECT- our baseline framework. This implies that AYT improves image quality while preserving image diversity, in accordance with our arguments above.

[1] Consistency Models, ICML, 2023.

**[W2] The notion of manifold feature is the center of the paper. However, it is not clearly validated. For example, does the level set $\phi^{-1}(\alpha)$ recover the data manifold?**

We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.4 of our revised paper, where we show that manifold feature level sets indeed approximate perturbed data manifolds by the method suggested by the Reviewer.

**[W3] I am a bit confused about the experiment setup, as far as I understand, the ECT does use a pretrained model and if the paper follows the same setup, then one cannot claim improvement over distillation-based models.**

We assure that ECT improves over distillation-based models in terms of both training efficiency and generative performance. For instance, Figure 2 in [1] shows that ECT requires less training compute and yields a better FID score compared to Consistency Distillation (CD).

Furthermore, as we show in Table 1 of our revised manuscript, AYT provides up to x3.9 acceleration in terms of wall-clock time over ECT, so our framework is even faster than CD in terms of training speed. Additionally, as shown in Table 3 of our revised manuscript, AYT vastly out-performs CD on 1-step generation: on CIFAR10, CD yields 3.55 FID and 9.48 IS whereas AYT yields 2.61 FID and 9.98 IS. On ImageNet 64x64, CD yields 6.20 FID while AYT yields 4.42 FID.

[1] Consistency Models Made Easy, ICLR, 2025.

summary.value: The paper studies consistency models (CMs), a 1-step distillation of diffusion models. It starts by proposing the following hypothesis: the tangent term in CMs' loss has oscillating behaviors (due to the data lying on low-dimensional manifold). The authors verify it with experiments on CIFAR10 and on a synthetic dataset. Based on this observation, the authors propose a feature map which removes oscillating behavior of the tangent and which makes the tangent more aligned to orthogonal components of the manifold.

strengths.value:
- Experiments on synthetic dataset in Section 4 are sound and convincing, particularly Figure 4. This is an interesting analysis of the CM's loss behavior. 

- Experimental results show improvements in 1-step generation for CMs when using the proposed method. 

- Experimental results show faster convergence of the generative model, although the compute budget of pre-training the classifiers is not considered.

weaknesses.value:
- Experiments on CIFAR10 in Section 4 are less convincing. It is only based on visualizations, which are not easily interpretable. I am uncertain if conclusions can be drawn from these visualizations. 

- Although the training of the generative model is faster, it relies on pre-training classifiers for the feature map construction. Moreover, it seems that it is required to train one classifier for each feature. This makes the overall pipeline complex, and the compute budget probably higher than in the original model.

questions.value: - To construct the several features, could you rely on a classifier with several heads?

> **The proposed solution requires feature engineering and thus might not be very generic (extension to other types of image datasets or other modalities is not guaranteed to work). That is why I do not raise my score to Accept.**

To address concerns about the applicability of our method to other domains or modalities, we additionally conducted experiments on the ImageNet 512×512 latent diffusion model (LDM). As shown in the Table below, AYT showed comparable improvements in FID and IS **without requiring substantial changes to the manifold feature training pipeline**. We refer the Reviewer to Appendix B.1 for a detailed explanation.

Given that our method demonstrates clear gains in the latent domain, we believe this indicates generalizable improvements across various image domains, and we further expect similar benefits to extend to other modalities such as audio and video. Moreover, because many modalities rely on latent autoencoders for generation [1,2,3], our findings on the ImageNet 512×512 LDM provide additional support for this expectation.
